sections.title: Defining the Sphere: From 1D to 3D
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a sphere not as a 'ball,' but as a set of points at a fixed distance 'R' from a center. Review the progression: a 1D sphere (two points), a 2D sphere (a circle), and a 3D sphere (the surface of a ball). Emphasize the boundary vs. the interior.
sections.example: Visualize a 'Point-Bot' moving on a line (1D), a flat plane (2D), and in a room (3D). The boundary is always one dimension lower than the space it inhabits.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Multi-Dimensional Pythagorean Theorem
sections.content: Transition to the mathematical definition. If a 2D circle is x² + y² = R² and a 3D sphere is x² + y² + z² = R², an n-sphere follows the pattern x₁² + x₂² + ... + xₙ² = R². This is simply the distance formula extended to n-coordinates.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Hyper-Ant' crawling in a 4D space. To find its distance from the origin, it just adds the square of its 4th coordinate to the usual 3D distance formula.

sections.title: The Volume Paradox: Shrinking to Zero
sections.content: Explore how the volume of a unit sphere (R=1) changes as dimensions (n) increase. Use a graph to show that volume increases until n=5, then starts decreasing rapidly toward zero. In infinite dimensions, the volume of a unit sphere vanishes.
sections.example: A 'Shape-Shifting Box': If you put a circle inside a square, it takes up most of the space. But as dimensions increase, a hyper-sphere inside a hyper-cube occupies almost none of the cube's volume—it becomes a 'ghost' shape.

sections.title: Surface Concentration: The 'Thin Crust' Effect
sections.content: Explain a counter-intuitive property: In high dimensions, almost all the volume of a sphere is located in a very thin shell near the surface. The interior is essentially empty.
sections.example: The 'High-D Orange': If you peel a 100-dimensional orange, even a paper-thin peel contains 99% of the fruit's mass. There is practically no 'meat' in the center of a high-dimensional orange.

sections.title: Applications: The Curse of Dimensionality
sections.content: Relate these geometric oddities to modern technology. High-dimensional spheres explain why 'Big Data' is difficult to process (points are always far apart) and how AI models organize information in vector spaces.
sections.example: A Recommendation Engine (like Netflix): Each movie is a point in a 1000-dimensional space. Because of sphere properties, most movies are 'equidistant' on the surface, making it hard to find a 'nearest neighbor' without clever math.

storyboard.title: Defining the Sphere: From 1D to 3D
lecture_lines: A sphere is all points at distance R from center.
In 1D, a sphere is just two points on line.
In 2D, a sphere is the boundary of circle.
In 3D, it is the surface of solid ball.
The boundary dimension is always one lower than space.
animations: Show a horizontal line (color #FFFFFF) with two points at distance 'r' from the center.
Transition the 1D line into a 2D circle (color #00FFFF) with radius 'r'.
Transition the 2D circle into a 3D sphere (color #FFD700) using shading to imply depth.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Multi-Dimensional Pythagorean Theorem
lecture_lines: Pythagorean theorem extends to any number of dimensions.
We sum the squares of all coordinate values.
This defines the distance to origin in n-dimensions.
animations: Display the 2D distance formula: x^2 + y^2 = r^2 (color #00FF00).
Transform the formula into the n-dimensional version: x_1^2 + x_2^2 +... + x_n^2 = R^2 (color #FFFF00).
Highlight the sum of squares with a flashing white box to emphasize the generalization.

storyboard.title: The Volume Paradox: Shrinking to Zero
lecture_lines: Unit sphere volume changes as dimensions increase.
Volume peaks at dimension five then starts decreasing.
In very high dimensions, the volume approaches zero.
Compare a sphere inside a high-dimensional cube.
The sphere occupies almost none of the cube's volume.
animations: Show the n-dimensional volume formula: V_n(R) = (pi^(n/2) / Gamma(n/2 + 1)) * R^n (color #FFFFFF).
Create a bar chart (color #00BFFF) showing volume for n=1 to n=10, where bars grow then shrink.
Animate the bars for n > 5 shrinking rapidly towards zero.
Display the text 'Volume -> 0' in bright green (#00FF00) as n increases.
Scale the 'Volume -> 0' text up and down to emphasize the paradox.

storyboard.title: Surface Concentration: The 'Thin Crust' Effect
lecture_lines: High-dimensional volume concentrates near the surface.
The interior of the sphere is mostly empty.
Imagine peeling a hundred-dimensional orange.
The thin peel contains nearly all the mass.
There is no 'meat' in a high-D orange.
animations: Show a unit circle (color #FFFFFF) with a concentric inner circle at radius 0.9 (color #FF4500).
Shade the area between the two circles (the 'crust') in orange (#FFA500).
Show a label 'High Dimension: Crust contains ~100% volume' in #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: Applications: The Curse of Dimensionality
lecture_lines: In high dimensions, points are usually far apart.
This makes searching and organizing big data difficult.
Geometry explains the challenges of modern AI models.
animations: Display a set of points scattered in a 2D square (color #FFFFFF).
Animate the points drifting apart to represent increasing sparsity in high dimensions.
Fade in the title 'Curse of Dimensionality' in bold red (#FF0000).
